analysis.one_liner: Requires businesses to show full prices up front and bans hidden junk fees in lodging, tickets, phone, and internet bills.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Commerce Committee from March 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required hotels, ticket sellers, internet and phone providers to show the total price — including all mandatory fees — the first time a consumer sees a price. It would have banned excessive or deceptive fees, barred early-termination fees on phone and internet plans, required airlines to seat children next to a parent at no extra charge, and given the FTC, the FCC, and state attorneys general power to enforce these rules. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers — concertgoers paying surprise 'service fees', travelers booking hotels or short-term rentals online, households with cable, internet, or cell bills padded with made-up line items, and families flying with young children who currently pay seat-selection fees to sit together.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers of lodging, tickets, telecom, air travel

how_it_helps.text: Requires lodging and ticketing businesses to display the total price including all mandatory fees in every ad and at first price display, and prohibits that price from changing during checkout [S2][S3].
Bans excessive or deceptive mandatory fees, with the FTC considering whether a fee is reasonable and proportional to the cost of the underlying good or service [S3].
Forces ticket sellers to disclose how many tickets they actually have before a sale, disclose refund policies, and warn buyers when they do not possess the ticket being sold [S2][S3].

Prohibits excessive or unreasonable early termination fees on internet, phone, and video services, and directs the FCC to consider banning or requiring disclosure of other mandatory fees in those bills [S2][S3].

Requires airlines to seat children 13 and under next to an accompanying adult at no extra charge, with a full refund or free rebooking if they cannot, and bans fees for family seating within the same cabin class [S2][S3].
Enforceable by the FTC, the FCC, and state attorneys general, who can sue for restitution and damages on behalf of their residents [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Industries whose revenue depends on junk fees: hotels and short-term rental platforms, ticketing companies and resellers, internet, mobile, and cable providers, and airlines that charge family seat-selection fees.

drawbacks.text: Businesses argue that regulating 'excessive' fees is vague and that fees reflect real costs, so a mandate could push costs into the headline price or reduce services [S3].
Banning early termination fees removes a device-financing tool telecoms use to subsidize 'free' phones, which could mean higher upfront prices for consumers [S3].
The family-seating requirement could complicate airline seat inventory, and airlines warn of operational costs if adjacent seats are scarce on full flights [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are broad and the compliance cost for businesses is comparatively small — showing the true total price up front does not eliminate fees, it just makes them visible before purchase. The strongest honest objection is vagueness: a ban on 'excessive' fees delegates a lot of judgment to the FTC and courts, and could invite litigation. On balance this is a consumer-protection bill whose costs fall on firms that currently profit from fees charged after the price is displayed.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in March 2023 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Blumenthal, joined by Sen. Whitehouse, introduced the Junk Fee Prevention Act in the Senate on March 22, 2023 [S1][S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
No further action appears in the record: the committee never held a hearing or voted, and the full Senate never considered it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill never reached a vote, so the businesses that collect junk fees — ticketing platforms, lodging and telecom providers, airlines charging family seating fees — kept the status quo. Consumers continue to pay hidden fees.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fee-charging industries; consumers kept paying hidden fees

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic sponsorship — Blumenthal with two Democratic cosponsors — and never reached a vote, so no one had to go on record against it.

industries.note: Must show all-in prices, disclose ticket holdbacks and speculative sales, and refund full amounts including fees — attacking the fee-heavy model of primary ticketers and resellers. Ticket service fees are a major add-on to already high ticket prices.
Must quote the total price including mandatory resort and cleaning fees from the first ad. These fees are a growing share of lodging revenue and currently appear late in the booking flow.
Early termination fees banned and the FCC directed to consider banning other mandatory fees that pad advertised prices. Telecom bills are a routine source of unexplained line-item charges.
Banned from charging family seat-selection fees and required to guarantee adjacent seating for children with a parent or refund. Seat fees are a fast-growing airline revenue stream.
